subject: Geni News for March 2026
body_text: Home of the World Family Tree New! Organize Your Research with the Geni Pro Workspace We are thrilled to unveil an exclusive new feature for our Geni Pro subscribers, the Geni Pro Workspace. The Geni Pro Workspace is a private, dedicated area to organize your family history research exactly how you want it. Whether you are deep in a research rabbit hole or just getting started on a new branch, the Geni Pro Workspace lets you capture notes, set to-dos, and manage your private projects without ever leaving Geni. Read more >> New Relationship Path Diagrams for Geni Pro Users We’re happy to announce an exciting new feature exclusive to Geni Pro subscribers – Relationship Path Diagrams! These easy-to-read visualizations offer a fresh way to explore how any two people are connected to others in the World Family Tree. Learn more >> Recapping the Magic of RootsTech 2026 We had an incredible time at RootsTech 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah. As the world’s largest genealogy conference, RootsTech always has a unique electricity in the air, and this year was no exception. Check out our full conference recap. Read more >> Your Wildest Family Stories Every family tree holds a few surprises. We asked the Geni community to share their wildest and most surprising family stories, and the responses reminded us why genealogy is more than just names and dates. It’s about moments, mysteries, and discoveries that bring our shared history to life. Read more >> Geni Tips: Use the Statistics Feature to Unlock Insights Into Your Family Tree Learn how Geni's Statistics feature can provide you with further insights into your family tree. It’s a hidden gem for anyone serious about family history research! Learn more >> Irish Genealogy Projects on Geni Do you have Irish ancestry? If you are trying to learn more about your Irish ancestors, Irish genealogy projects on Geni are a fantastic way to collaborate and connect with others who are also researching their Irish roots. Explore these Irish genealogy related projects on Geni! Read more >> A Look Back at 2025 on Geni From new features to a major milestone for the World Family Tree, 2025 was filled with discoveries, collaboration, and connections that brought family history to life. Join us as we revisit some of the highlights that made 2025 a year to remember on Geni. Read more >> Log In to Geni You are currently signed up to receive Geni company news. subject: Learning Spotlight: AI That Works for You
body_text:
AI Skills That Matter Now

AI can draft an email, analyze a quarter's worth of data, or build a working app from a single prompt. But knowing what to askmdashand how to apply the resultsmdashis what turns capability into real value. Whether you're just getting started or already experimenting, these expert-led courses help you put it to work.


 
All the best!
Shea Hanson, Head of Learning Content Strategy, LinkedIn Learning

Devlin Peck posted: One week ago I opened the waitlist for devlin.ai, my new AI-powered simulation builder for learning teams.

I would've been happy if 30 people signed up.  

But over 200 instructional designers, learning managers, and L&D executives registered in less than 7 days. 

This project started as a way to help my Peck Academy students create AI simulations more easily, but I think it struck a bigger nerve in the industry.

People are sharing major pain points, like how branching logic takes forever to build. And how scenarios can come across as scripted instead of feeling like real conversations.  

The biggest pain is that learners end up clicking through multiple-choice options instead of practicing how they'd respond in real life.

These are the exact problems that devlin.ai solves, even though I didn't realize it in the beginning.

Here's how it works: 

You describe a scenario and the AI handles the conversation dynamically. Learners type or speak naturally. The AI responds in character. You get analytics on how they performed.   

You don't have to deal with JavaScript or API keys, and the simulation exports as SCORM or HTML (and embeds directly into Storyline, Rise, or any LMS). 

My favorite part is that the AI simulation can update Storyline variables in real-time, letting you change character facial expressions, play sound effects, show pass/fail screens, and so much more.

Today, all 200+ waitlist members got access, and I couldn't be more excited to see what they create.  

I also recorded a 6-minute walkthrough of the tool for the new users. I figured I'd share it here so you can see the progress.

Finally, if you missed the first wave and want access when the next one opens, join the waitlist with the link in the comments.

This has been one of the most energizing weeks I've had in a long time. Thank you to everyone who signed up early and shared feedback.

Let's do this thing.

#LinkedInWithDevlin #InstructionalDesign #eLearning #ArtificialIntelligence #LearningAndDevelopment

subject: Troy Gunawardene posted: I got invited to a conference for folks with my job…
body_text:
Troy Gunawardene posted: I got invited to a conference for folks with my job title. I was probably the only teenager in the room...

Last week, I had the opportunity to attend The FDE Conference II, an event held by Nixo (YC S25), Rippling, and ElevenLabs about the future of the intersection between software engineering and product management - in other words, Forward-Deployed Engineers.

Before starting my current co-op at Ranger, I had never actually met an FDE. In fact, I had never even heard of the title before applying. But last Tuesday, I was in a room full of them. 

I got to hear insights from speakers like Leo Mehr, John Chang, Kevin Bai - people who are leaders and pioneers of the Forward-Deployed model - and it's exciting to imagine the role FDEs will play in the crazy new world of AI-driven-everything that we're being thrust into.

Looking forward to attending more events in the bay!

(Note: it's the gradient-cover, paperback edition that says "revised and updated" on the cover.) Besides some refreshed examples in the original 10 chapters, it comes with two brand spankin’ new sections on Managing Remotely and Managing in a Downturn. In the years since publication I lamented not having addressed these two topics more deeply, especially after the pandemic and the various market downturns and layoffs we’ve seen. My current hot take is that in the era of AI, You're definitely going to be a manager now! (Topic of my latest blog post, linked to in my header). Why? Well, let's start by asking: what is the skill of management? In my book I define it as getting better outcomes from a group by the use of three key levers: purpose (aligning on what success looks like), people (defining who is needed to achieve the goal), and process (defining how the work should get done). Now imagine that formerly large Avengers team being compressed into one or two Captain Marvels, thanks to AI. The headcount shrinks, but the need to manage work doesn’t. Those remaining individuals have to think like managers in deciding what to prioritize, how to split tasks, and how to keep themselves accountable. In other words, certain parts of the management function must shift into the hands of the Individual Contributor. This is why there’s so much chatter about how AI rewards high-agency people with a clear sense of purpose (some great reads on what “high agency” is here and here). Instead of waiting for someone else to help coordinate or define next steps, these folks experiment quickly, learn and share. Instead of expecting coaching and feedback from humans, an IC can ask, Help me critique this presentation or Point out blind spots in my argument and get an instant second opinion from AI. AI also gives ICs better tools to improve collaboration with other humans. Worried about how to tell a colleague that their proposal sucks? Have AI help you draft a direct-yet-kind script and roleplay the conversation with you. Trying to make sure your higher-ups know what’s up? Have AI draft you clean exec summaries. The old boundary lines are blurring. Just as we’ll see fewer “pure managers,” we’ll also see fewer “pure ICs.” Instead, more people will live in the messy middle: sometimes executing, sometimes designing processes, sometimes coordinating. Like switching hats in a fast-moving improv show, the distinction between manager and IC becomes less about rigid role definitions and more about moment-to-moment needs.  Comment:https://www.linkedin.com/comm/feed/update/activity:7371281966521880576?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_notification_digest_01%3BDUQxfwwQRXSOwrUN2M1VcA%3D%3D&midToken=AQHfHWFtsZSaww&midSig=2skna6jxk-YHU1&trk=eml-email_notification_digest_01-notification_digest-0-SHARED_BY_YOUR_NETWORK&trkEmail=eml-email_notification_digest_01-notification_digest-0-SHARED_BY_YOUR_NETWORK-null-j3xwl4~mfd8th1x~o7-null-null&eid=j3xwl4-mfd8th1x-o7&otpToken=MTMwNDFiZTUxNjI5YzFjNGIzMmMwZmViNDExYmUwYjA4OWNhZDI0MjlhYTg4OTYyN2JjZjA2Njk0ZjVhNWNmMmY0ZDZkNGU5NThkOGJiZjMwMGFlZDVjM2FmZGIyZWE5M2Q1YWQyNjM0ZDdiOWE0NTI1MDA3MDgwLDEsMQ%3D%3D Vincent Tran posted: 🔔 All day, I have random alert notification sounds coming from various apps and browser windows. Well, we opened Duo’s Taqueria because we want to connect with people. 

Obviously, we want our employees to connect, so Duo’s Taqueria offers free food 🌮🥑 and drinks 🍹 for our employees once a week. 

But much less obviously, we want to connect 🫂 with our community in Pittsburgh. 

The tech bubble is real, and we don’t want to live in it. The taqueria gives our local community and our employees a chance to get to know each other and develop relationships. 💚

Read more ⬇️ about how our CEO Luis von Ahn's craving for tacos inspired Duo’s Taqueria.

Then lastly, the best fellow interns I could ask for: Akshar Koul, Dharana Alilaikannan, Kevin Morales, Jacob Kerby, Ryan Hughes, and Preston W..

Thank you, Early Warning®!

Instead, you need to have trusted, highly personalized conversations with your prospects. Not sure where to start? Here are five phrases to drop from your pitch and what to say instead. Munachimso Nwugo posted: Overengineering is fun. Really, you should try it sometime.

There's a certain joy that comes from devising solutions that are way too complex for problems that few would even consider problems at all. All fun and games when the stakes are low.

But when the stakes are high... well, let's just say it's easy to shoot yourself in the foot. And by that, I mean blow your whole leg to oblivion.

A few weeks into my current internship, a tech lead called me into a room and introduced me to EEPROM wear levelling. A classic embedded engineering problem, with only one caveat: I've never come near embedded engineering a day in my life. To me, it was dark magic (memory management) and cryptic cyphers (bit mathematics). The perfect opportunity to display my aptitude for overly complex problems!

It was a disaster.

My entire meticulously crafted plan fell apart in a single review. Too many moving parts, too many failure modes, and a dawning realisation that I should probably leave the overengineering in my projects.

Because when the stakes are real, simplicity is king. 

P.S -  Below is a shameless plug to the 'simple' solution I landed on, which, let's be honest, is still a little bit overengineered. Old habits do, indeed, die hard!

Sean Finch commented on Kaan Onarlioglu’s post: I think teaching how to effectively use it as a tool could be helpful, but I don't see how it could become an integral part of syssec, unless I'm missing something. Using it as guidance when you get stuck could prove useful for some students, but my general take on AI is that we (both as a society and students) have become too reliant on it.

There's a new study that shows that technology use in schools in adolescence correlates directly with lower test scores. I fear that encouraging the use of AI in classes could lead down a slippery slope and lower overall critical thinking. Our generation was the first to grow up with Web 2. Now that we are becoming adults, I think we are beginning to realize how much of a detriment all that unrestricted access to technology has been. Stricter limits on screentime and access would've done us all good, and taught us moderation before we became adults.

But all of that is a much larger discussion to be had at a Khoury, university, and even government level. I think it would be best to strike a balance of teaching students how to use LLMs in syssec effectively, and in moderation, without mandating it and risking losing the technical concepts taught in the course.

Rich Zou posted: I used to wash dishes in my mom’s restaurant.

She ran it for over 20 years in the heart of Chinatown, NYC.
Single mom. Immigrant. Worked 12+ hours a day, 7 days a week.

We didn’t grow up with much, but she taught me two things that stuck:
Be kind. Be honest.

That restaurant was my first lesson in hustle.
I was the dishwasher. Then the cashier.
Eventually, I found ways to make money on my own -
reselling sneakers.
Streaming as a pro gamer.
Trying any side hustle I could find.

When I got to college, I thought I had to follow the traditional AAPI path:
Finance. Consulting. Prestige.

But the truth?
I got rejected from every VC fellowship.
Didn’t land the fancy internships.
Felt completely lost.

Last semester, I left Boston-where all my friends were-and flew to SF with no real plan. No job. No network. No safety net.

But sometimes all it takes is one believer.

That’s when I met Anne.
She gave me a shot.
5 weeks into interning at Parable, and I’ve already learned more than any class could teach.
Not just about venture — but about people, conviction, and how the best founders really think.

Anne is the definition of founder-first.
If you’re building in consumer — you should talk to her.

As for me - I’ll keep working 10x harder. I still feel like the underdog.
But I know where I came from.
And I know where I want to go.

If you’ve ever felt behind, unseen, or unsure where to start - I’ve been there.
And if you want to chat, learn about my journey, or get advice on anything from writing LinkedIn posts to navigating career stuff…

Try out my digital twin on Delphi - I made sure it sounds exactly like me.

LinkedIn News shared a post: Is it better to live near work opportunities or family?

Last week, we shared LinkedIn survey data showing that 53% of Americans currently live within one hour of their closest family member, and the latest cut reveals how this differs by generation.

Gen Z workers were the most likely to say they live less than one hour away from their closest family members (59%), compared to the U.S. average of 53%. Baby boomers were the next most likely to live near family, followed by Gen X and millennials.

Among the survey respondents who have moved away from home, millennials were most likely to say their decision to move was motivated by hopes of career advancement — either their own or a partner’s.

Though millennial workers are least likely to live near their hometowns, and most likely to have moved away for their careers, when it comes to Gen Zers, it’s possible that a lack of savings and rising costs of living are keeping them closer to home.

Siya Patel shared a post: Exciting recap of our latest event! 🎬

On Thursday 11/21, BOE had the pleasure of hosting Brynne Norquist and Tyler Knohl, the founders of Hiike, a platform for connecting filmmakers to film festivals. They shared their experiences founding a company as college students and how they are actively transforming the entertainment industry.

Some key takeaways from the event were:
- Identifying a niche by addressing the disconnect between film festivals and filmmakers
- Leveraging data to drive their processes and exploring the intersection of data science and the entertainment industry
- Overcoming fears of AI, learning how to leverage it, and using it to help independent filmmakers gain a competitive edge

We cannot wait to see how Hiike revolutionizes the entertainment industry and empowers filmmakers nationwide!

LinkedIn News shared a post: If only the toy business was child's play. Instead, it's one of the most unforgiving of industries: The embodiment of what-have-you-done-for-me-lately, where products endure for maybe a season (if at all), where brands which delight generation after generation of children are few and far between.

Even if you're Mattel, Inc., a company so well known it is an outlier in the toy space – Quick! Name another — one that delights children with toys everybody knows, among them Barbie, Hot Wheels and American Girl.

And yet, when Ynon Kreiz took over as CEO in 2018 as the company's fourth CEO in four years — the previous three all resigned — the 80-year-old company wasn't doing very well. But Kreiz was already on the board, a perch which gave him enough exposure to Mattel's problems for him to reach a game-changing conclusion: Customers don't just buy this toy or that. They're not even customers. They're fans. They're … an audience.

In this edition of This is Working, Kreiz talks about how the Barbie movie came together, how he hires, fires and reassigns, and his three chief management principles

To keep up with these conversations and be inspired by the world’s top leaders, subscribe to This is Working: linkedin.com/thisisworking

Vivian Zou shared a post: This month, I had the opportunity to present a project that my groupmates Gillian Palmer, Qihong Wu, and Ahan Jain spent this semester developing at the Oasis showcase at Northeastern University. 

Our project, Husky Laundry, aims to facilitate real-time monitoring of laundry machines across Northeastern dorms. Our application allows the user to search for laundry rooms in their dorms and see which machines are currently available, are in use, or are out of order. We also implemented a time bar below each of the machines to indicate how much longer the machine would be in use. By filtering and sorting the machines and rooms, we enhance the user experience and focus on the usability of our product. We additionally developed a Problems page, allowing users to report any issues they encounter with the machines.

Throughout the four months that we worked on this project, I was fortunate to learn more about web development and what it takes to create a full-stack application. I am so grateful to have this opportunity to work with Oasis and my group members, together we persevered and learned crucial skills while developing an engaging project. 

Lastly, we wish to give a special thank you to Xiaole Su for her contribution to the sprites showcased in our final product and Kenny Jung for being an amazing mentor and guide throughout the project.

Neil Blumenthal, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of Warby Parker certainly believes so!

“About a billion people around the planet don't have glasses,” he explains. “So we thought, well, what could we do through business to help solve this broader problem?”

Amazon shared a post: Tomorrow is International Dog Day, and we are celebrating all of our beloved office dogs. 🦮 🐩 🐕🦺 🐕 

Amazon has been ranked among the most dog-friendly companies in the U.S.

It all started with Rufus the corgi. In the early days of Amazon.com, a husband and wife team brought their Welsh corgi, Rufus, to work with them, and he became a surprisingly productive part of the team. Employees would even use Rufus's paw to click the computer mouse to launch some of the earliest pages of Amazon.com.

Rufus's memory is still honored at Amazon: There are photos of him around the Puget Sound campus, and there's even a building in South Lake Union that was named after him.

And now, thousands of office dogs follow in Rufus's paw steps. 🐾 

Having dogs in our workplace has been found to lower stress and boost morale, and we're proud this is such a uniquely Amazonian tradition.

Amazon shared a post: Tomorrow is International Dog Day, and we are celebrating all of our beloved office dogs. 🦮 🐩 🐕🦺 🐕 

Amazon has been ranked among the most dog-friendly companies in the U.S.

It all started with Rufus the corgi. In the early days of Amazon.com, a husband and wife team brought their Welsh corgi, Rufus, to work with them, and he became a surprisingly productive part of the team. Employees would even use Rufus's paw to click the computer mouse to launch some of the earliest pages of Amazon.com.

Rufus's memory is still honored at Amazon: There are photos of him around the Puget Sound campus, and there's even a building in South Lake Union that was named after him.

And now, thousands of office dogs follow in Rufus's paw steps. 🐾 

Having dogs in our workplace has been found to lower stress and boost morale, and we're proud this is such a uniquely Amazonian tradition.

We would love to see a photo of your dog in the office in the comments! 🔽
